summary: Submits an idea for using IP and ARP on mixed FDDI networks that contain both single-MAC and dual-MAC stations, by introducing a new protocol layer. It is informational and offers a proposal, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo suggests how two computers with two network connections each could send data over both connections at the same time. A new helper layer does the address work, so IP and the usual address lookup do not have to change.

subtitle: A proposal for a load sharing layer that lets dual MAC FDDI stations use both rings while ARP and IP stay unchanged.

tldr.problem: On an FDDI network that mixes single MAC and dual MAC stations, ARP learns only one hardware address per station, so two dual MAC stations cannot use both of their rings.
tldr.mechanism: A new load sharing layer sits under ARP and IP in dual MAC stations. It uses the Dual MAC Address Resolution Protocol (DMARP) to exchange secondary MAC addresses on the secondary ring, and it keeps an address cache that decides which ring carries each IP frame.
tldr.outcome: Two dual MAC stations on the same ring pair could split their traffic and reach 200 Mbits/s, with no change to single MAC stations or transparent bridges. The memo is an Informational RFC that offers an idea rather than a standard, and it has been updated by RFC 5494.

today: RFC 1329 is an Informational RFC from May 1992. It submits an idea rather than a standard, and it has been updated by RFC 5494. The memo says that security issues are not discussed in it.

sections.title: The Problem and the Proposal
sections.content:
An FDDI network has a primary ring and a secondary ring. A single MAC station attaches one network interface to the primary ring. A dual MAC station has two, one on each ring, and each one has its own hardware address, as the FDDI station management standard requires. If two dual MAC stations sit on the same ring pair, they could send some of their traffic down each ring and use the double bandwidth of 200 Mbits/s. ARP gets in the way: it learns one hardware address per station, and only the primary one.

The memo's answer is a new protocol layer that exists only in dual MAC stations. It sits between ARP and IP on one side and the two stacks of SNAP, LLC and MAC on the other. It gives ARP the same interface that SNAP gives it, so ARP, IP and everything above them cannot tell that the station has two interfaces. The layer exchanges the missing secondary addresses with a second protocol, the Dual MAC Address Resolution Protocol (DMARP), which runs alongside the ordinary ARP exchange. Single MAC stations and transparent bridges need no change at all.

The memo makes three assumptions. When the dual ring wraps, both interfaces of a dual MAC station are assumed to stay connected. The interface of a single MAC station is assumed to sit on the primary ring. Transparent bridges may link rings to other LANs or to further inhomogeneous FDDI rings, but none is allowed between a primary ring and a secondary ring.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers on an FDDI ring have two network connections and some have one. This memo suggests how the two-connection computers can send data over both connections at once, using a helper layer that leaves the usual software alone.

sections.title: The Load Sharing Layer
sections.content:
In a single MAC station, IP sits on ARP, ARP sits on the Subnetwork Access Protocol (SNAP), SNAP sits on 802.2 Logical Link Control (LLC) type 1, which offers a connectionless service, and LLC sits on the FDDI MAC. The memo investigates connectionless service only.

In a dual MAC station, the new load sharing layer sits between ARP and two separate stacks. On one side there is SNAP 1, LLC 1 and the primary MAC, which reaches the primary ring. On the other there is SNAP 2, LLC 2 and the secondary MAC, which reaches the secondary ring. ARP frames travel towards the primary side and IP frames can travel towards either one, depending on what the layer decides.

Inside the layer sits one load sharing entity with three parts: the address cache, the cache administration and the multiplexer. The cache holds the primary and secondary MAC addresses of other dual MAC stations, and there are no entries for single MAC stations. The load sharing entities in different stations talk to each other with DMARP to exchange addresses and reachability information. DMARP frames travel inside a SNAP header whose Organizationally Unique Identifier is set to zero, and whose 16-bit EtherType field holds a new number for DMARP that the memo says is not defined yet.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper layer looks to ARP just like the SNAP layer does, so ARP keeps sending and receiving frames exactly as before. The layer keeps a table of the other two-connection stations it has met, and a separate small protocol fills that table in.

sections.title: Learning Secondary Addresses with DMARP
sections.content:
ARP may only know the addresses of MACs on the primary ring, so the load sharing layer always hands ARP frames to SNAP 1 for transmission. Communication with ARP therefore happens over the primary ring in the normal state, and the ARP cache holds no secondary MAC addresses. A secondary MAC can still receive an ARP frame when the dual ring is wrapped and the destination hardware address is a multicast or broadcast address; those frames are discarded because they arrived twice.

To learn secondary addresses, the layer sends a DMARP reply frame on the secondary ring every time it hands an ARP frame to SNAP 1. The reply carries the sending station's own primary and secondary MAC addresses, it is addressed to the broadcast MAC address, and it copies the IP destination address from the ARP frame it travels beside. If that ARP frame was a request, the ARP entity in the receiving station answers with an ARP reply, and the reply in turn makes the layer send a DMARP reply on the secondary ring. The two exchanges therefore run in parallel.

Two dual MAC stations on different dual FDDI rings joined by a single transparent bridge cannot share load, because no DMARP reply gets from one secondary ring to the other. The station marks that cache entry with the OR-bit, the other ring bit, and does no load sharing with it. A timer later sends a DMARP request to the secondary MAC address and discards the entry, so the entry can be learned again if the network has changed, and a DMARP error frame guards against a lost reply. On large networks a ring is more likely to be wrapped when two stations first meet, which makes load sharing look possible when it is not. The memo adds control bits for that case: a read-only R-bit for entries written by hand, a Hold bit that marks a load sharing as trusted and is checked later by query and hold frames, and search and found frames that let a third station confirm a possible load sharing between two others.
sections.plainLanguage: Each time a station sends an address lookup on the main ring, it also sends its second address on the other ring. Other two-connection stations then know where to reach it on both rings. If the two stations turn out to be on separate rings, they stop sharing the load.

sections.title: The Address Cache, the Multiplexer and the Timers
sections.content:
The address cache holds one entry per other dual MAC station. Each entry stores a 48-bit primary MAC address, a 48-bit secondary MAC address, a 32-bit subscript that identifies the entry, the 16-bit protocol type last used with that station, and six control bits. LS says a load sharing can be performed with the station, OR says no load sharing may be done with it because it is on another ring, H says the load sharing is trusted, Q says a query was sent and no hold frame came back, R says DMARP cannot change the entry, and V says the entry is valid. LS and OR always hold inverted values, so one of them is redundant, but both are defined to make checking the state of an entry easier. The protocol type number and the address lengths are taken over from ARP, which lets a dual MAC station speak DMARP with a station that does not use IP at all.

The multiplexer decides which ring carries each outgoing IP frame. Broadcast and multicast frames always go on the primary ring, because one of the addressed stations could be a single MAC station. If there is no cache entry for the destination, the frame also goes on the primary ring. If there is an entry and the LS bit is set, a load sharing criterion picks the ring; the memo leaves that criterion open and gives the length of the transmit queues in the MACs as an example. Multicast and broadcast frames received from the secondary MAC are discarded, so they are not delivered twice.

The cache administration needs three timers, and only one of them runs at a time for each cache entry. The OR-Entry-Timer runs for OR-set-timeout, which the memo says should be some 10 seconds and should be much longer than the time a frame needs to travel around the whole network. The Hold-Timer runs for Hold-time, the period within which the frames of a first exchange must arrive before a load sharing is assumed to work; the memo proposes several minutes. The Query-Timer runs for Query-time, the period after which the H bit is checked by sending a query frame and waiting for a hold frame back; the memo also proposes several minutes for this. Section 10 restates the whole load sharing entity as a formal description written in ESTELLE, with the multiplexer and the cache administration as separate modules and the timer services as channel calls.
sections.plainLanguage: The layer keeps a table of the other two-connection stations, with flags that say whether traffic can be split between them. A small rule then sends each outgoing message down the main ring or the other one, and timers clear out entries that no longer work.

sections.title: The DMARP Frame
sections.content:
A DMARP frame reuses the ARP layout. It carries a 16-bit hardware type, where 1 means "ethernet"; a 16-bit protocol type, 2048 for the Internet Protocol; an 8-bit length of the hardware addresses, which is 6 octets for a 48-bit MAC address; an 8-bit length of the protocol addresses, which is 4 octets for an Internet address; a 16-bit operation field; and then the two hardware addresses followed by the sender's and the receiver's protocol addresses.

The operation field has seven values: 1 reply, 2 request, 3 error, 4 search, 5 found, 6 query and 7 hold. A reply, request or error frame carries the sender's primary and secondary MAC addresses. A search frame carries the sender's primary MAC address and the counter station's primary MAC address. A found frame carries the sender's primary MAC address and the counter station's secondary MAC address. A query frame carries the sender's secondary MAC address and the counter station's primary MAC address. A hold frame carries the sender's primary and secondary MAC addresses.

Apart from error frames, all DMARP frames travel on the secondary ring. Reply, error and search frames are addressed to the broadcast hardware address. Request, found, query and hold frames are addressed to an individual secondary MAC address.
sections.plainLanguage: A DMARP frame looks like an ARP frame with a number added that says what kind of message it is: a reply, a request, an error, a search, a found, a query or a hold. Every message but an error one goes out on the second ring.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo states in one line that security issues are not discussed in it. Nothing in the described protocol authenticates the stations that answer DMARP frames, and nothing protects a cache entry from a station that answers with the wrong addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says nothing about security. It does not describe any check that the station answering an address message is the station it claims to be.

fields.name: Operation
fields.desc: 1 reply, 2 request, 3 error, 4 search, 5 found, 6 query, 7 hold.

fields.name: First Hardware Address
fields.desc: Sender or counter station address, depending on the operation.

fields.name: Second Hardware Address
fields.desc: Sender or counter station address, depending on the operation.

items.label: reply
items.desc: Carries the sender's primary and secondary MAC addresses. Sent to the broadcast address.

items.label: request
items.desc: Asks a station to send a reply. Sent to its secondary MAC address.

items.label: error
items.desc: Used when a DMARP reply gets lost on the ring.

items.label: search
items.desc: Carries the sender's primary MAC address and the counter station's primary MAC address. Sent to the broadcast address.

items.label: found
items.desc: A third station reports a sure load sharing. Sent to a secondary MAC address.

items.label: query
items.desc: Checks that the Hold bit is still correct. Sent to a secondary MAC address.

items.label: hold
items.desc: Acknowledges a query. Sent to a secondary MAC address.
